reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Results from dysfunction of one or more spinal nerve roots, producing pain, sensory change, and weakness in a dermatomal and myotomal distribution
Pain characteristically radiates along the affected root and is often aggravated by manoeuvres that raise intraspinal pressure such as coughing or straining
The commonest cause is a degenerative disc or spondylotic osteophyte compressing the root within or near the intervertebral foramen
Localising signs follow the root: for example L5 causes foot-drop with weak dorsiflexion, while S1 reduces the ankle reflex and plantar flexion
Provocative tests such as straight-leg raise (lumbar) or Spurling manoeuvre (cervical) support a root cause
Most cases are self-limiting and improve with conservative management, so imaging is guided by red flags and by persistence or progression of deficits
MRI is the preferred imaging test to correlate structural compression with the clinical level
Electromyography helps confirm the affected root and distinguish radiculopathy from plexopathy or peripheral neuropathy
reference.pathophysiology: Radiculopathy reflects mechanical compression, inflammation, or ischaemia of a nerve root, most often where a herniated disc or degenerative spondylotic change narrows the intervertebral foramen or lateral recess. Compression and local inflammatory mediators disrupt axonal conduction and cause both ectopic pain signals and conduction failure, producing radicular pain, dermatomal sensory loss, and myotomal weakness. Chronic compression may lead to axonal loss with denervation. Non-degenerative causes include infection, malignant infiltration, and inflammatory or infiltrative processes affecting the roots.
additionalDifferentials: Referred pain from shoulder, hip, or joint disease
Infective or neoplastic root involvement (e.g. epidural abscess, metastasis, meningeal disease)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the relevant spinal region to identify compressive pathology
CT or CT myelography when MRI is contraindicated
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to localise the root and exclude mimics
Inflammatory markers and imaging for infection or malignancy when red flags are present
Plain radiographs for alignment, instability, or degenerative change in selected cases
redFlags: New bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, or bilateral leg symptoms suggesting cauda equina syndrome (surgical emergency)
Progressive or severe motor weakness rather than isolated pain
Fever, systemic illness, or immunosuppression raising concern for spinal infection
History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, or night pain suggesting malignant infiltration
reference.prognosis: Most degenerative radiculopathies resolve or substantially improve with conservative treatment over weeks to a few months; persistent severe compression, marked motor deficit, or a serious underlying cause predicts a poorer outcome and may require surgery.
pitfalls: Missing cauda equina syndrome by not asking about sphincter and saddle symptoms
Over-reliance on incidental imaging findings that do not match the clinical level
Attributing radicular pain to a benign disc when infection or malignancy is the true cause
Delaying surgical referral in progressive motor weakness
Confusing peripheral entrapment or plexopathy with root disease without electrophysiology
management: First-line conservative care with analgesia, neuropathic pain agents, activity modification and physiotherapy, as most degenerative radiculopathies settle
Image-guided epidural or transforaminal corticosteroid injection for persistent radicular pain
Surgical decompression such as discectomy or foraminotomy for progressive or severe motor deficit or intractable pain
Directed treatment of a non-degenerative cause, with antimicrobials for infection or oncological therapy for malignant root infiltration
Monitoring of neurological deficits with urgent escalation for progressive weakness or features of cauda equina compression
Imaging guided by red flags and by persistence or progression of symptoms rather than routine early scanning
